Chapter 4: The Role of Policy and the Power of Intervention
Sometimes, the rules of the game just change—almost overnight. Wars, crises, big political movements... they can shake everything up, forcing society to rethink who gets what, and why. If you look back at the 20th century, you'll find plenty of moments when governments stepped in and rewrote the playbook for wealth and income.
After the devastation of the world wars, countries faced a huge decision. Old fortunes were wiped out, and rebuilding was urgent. So, what did governments do? They raised taxes on the rich, launched social programs, and started investing in public goods. And for a while, it really worked. Inequality dropped, and suddenly, more people believed a better life was actually possible. The dream of progress felt real.
But here’s something to pay attention to—these changes didn’t just happen by chance. They came from tough political decisions, sparked by the pressures of war and the voices of everyday people. High taxes on income, wealth, and inheritance slowed down the rise of new fortunes. Social safety nets gave people more security. Investments in education and health? They opened doors that had been shut for generations.
Of course, nothing stays the same forever. As the memories of crisis faded, so did the pressure for equality. Governments started cutting taxes on the rich and trimming social programs. Slowly, the old patterns crept back in. Wealth began to concentrate at the top, and the gap between rich and poor widened again. The logic of capital—the way money seems to multiply for those who already have it—took hold once more.
But you know, the story of policy isn’t just about numbers or charts. It’s about values—about the kind of society people want to build, and what they’re willing to do to get there. When governments act, they really can change the rules. But those changes? They’re always up for debate, shaped by politics and the balance of power at any moment.
In recent decades, globalization and technology have completely transformed the landscape. Some people hoped these changes would make things fairer, open up opportunities for everyone. But when you look at the evidence, the old rule still holds: capital keeps growing faster than the economy. And without intervention, inequality just keeps rising.
So, here’s the key takeaway. If we just let capitalism run its course, big gaps between rich and poor are almost guaranteed. But it doesn’t have to be that way. Policy choices—about taxes, social programs, and economic rules—can make a real difference. The real question is, are we willing to act? And what kind of future do we want to create?
